The one thing that keeps me from being 100% certain about the crypto bottom (I don't think anyone can ever be certain at the time) is I know how absolutely brutal this asset class is. 

We have historically always absolutely fucked over everyone by going much lower than consensus.

This is what I believe is currently creating a lingering disbelief. 

Every bear market we find all the reasons why this time will be different, and it was never different. This time around we have more reasons than ever in the age of ETFs, macro, and other data points.

Despite being fully aware of this, I decided to throw my hat into bull camp on the break of 65k alongside Bessent's bond intervention, which my gut told me was a kind of white swan, and almost echoed with what Satoshi inscribed in the genesis block "chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks" etc. 

10/10 was probably the worst crypto event I've witnessed in terms of the speed of destruction. 

I watched the covid crash, which was at least a bit telegraphed in advance, obviously brutal as well...
But, 10/10 just randomly sent all alt coins 80% down in like 20 minutes, and carried out everyone who was running any sort of leverage. 

So, it does seem quite extreme when I consider another black swan type event alongside 10/10 in the space of a year to create us a lower low. And I think we would need something very bad to get back down below $60k. 

Even for the crypto script writers that would be quite nasty stuff. 

Yes, I can see all the historical patterns, and how it could happen, and the "why assume anything is different crowd" have always done well with that logic. 

That being said, each cycle is actually slightly different, and markets do in fact change. The profile of Bitcoin as an asset has certainly changed from the last few cycles.

As someone that always prioritises survival, I have a few bullets still ready to fire, but I wasn't a greedy bear and have my spot bag exposure already. I loaded on the alts I wanted regardless of BTC. 

I can still weather a storm if it comes, and will ride it out no matter what.

I think once we get deeper into Q4 and 2027 we will have a lot to feel optimistic about. 

Just a few thoughts out loud, as maybe it will resonate with a few of you thinking the same thing.

One of the best charter schools in the country, Success Academy, just filed suit against the NYS Department of Education Commissioner Betty Rosa for no longer permitting the College Board from disclosing AP exam results from NYS schools. 

For years, NYSED had permitted the College Board to share aggregate, non-personally identifying data on Advanced Placement (AP) exams with U.S. News & World Report, as 47 other states have also done, so that U.S. News could develop its national ranking of all public high schools. This year, Commissioner Rosa blocked the College Board from providing AP data to U.S. News preventing SA’s data from being released.

The AP exam disclosure is important as it plays a significant role in school rankings nationwide. Success Academy in previous years was ranked 11th in NYS and 9th in NYC last year, the highest of any school that does not have selective admissions. Without the AP data this year, Success Academy’s ranking dropped to 196th statewide and the school’s and its students extraordinary outperformance thereby has gone unrecognized. 

Success Academy does not limit demanding AP coursework to a small, academically elite group — all of its students (who win admission by lottery) have access to challenging, college-level academic work. And they have produced exceptional AP results. 

This year, more than 3,000 SA students took 7,810 AP examinations across 18 subjects—with an average pass rate of 68 percent. Nationally, fewer than 25 percent of high school students pass even one AP examination by the time they graduate. 

At Success, 95 percent of its 2026 graduating class passed three or more AP examinations, 79 percent passed five or more, and 60 percent passed seven or more. They outperformed their New York and global peers on nine AP examinations, including U.S. and European History, Macroeconomics, Microeconomics, and Literature.

Ask yourself why NYSED Commissioner Betty Rosa would choose to limit the release of student performance data on APs. 

By doing so, she diminishes the performance of the best charter schools, masking the poor performance of NYS and NYC public schools, and limiting the recognition of Success’ and other great charter schools’ faculty and students. 

The UFT teachers union recently sued Success Academy for ostensibly violating the Charter cap, which prevents Success, the largest NYC charter school operator, from opening new schools. 

So here in America, the teachers union working with the NYSED is using litigation and concealment of data to prevent our kids from getting a better education and keep parents in the dark. 

This should be a crime, and Betty Rosa should be ashamed of herself. 

(I have cribbed sections of some of the language and data above from a letter from Success Academy’s Founder & CEO Eva Moskowitz. If X had footnotes I would have added them.)

6. All actions sit natively in the lending market, so all positions are always earning yield (irrespective of a resting or executed order).
